latin_text: Cum reperietur ejus sarcophagum integrum, illibatum, in futuris temporibus videbitur; et erit apertum toto orbi terrarum. Et tunc nec aqua nec ros cœli insulam nobilissimam habitantibus poterit deficere. Per multum tempus ante diem judicialem in Josaphat erant aperta hæc et viventibus declarata.” Hunc Mevinum Britannum chronographum appellat Johannes Hardingus in chronico suo poemate, pro quo Nenii nomen, capite octavo et quadragesimo irrepsit : ubi bellam istam ex eo recitat fabellam, quod Josephus Arvirago regi pro gentis Britannicæ insignibus crucem, quæ Georgiana postea dicta est, in clypeo argenteo depictam tradiderit.

translation_history.english: When his sarcophagus shall be found entire, intact, in time to come, it shall be seen; and shall be open unto all the world. Thenceforth nor water nor the dew of heaven shall fail the dwellers in that ancient isle. "For a long while before the Day of Judgment in Josaphat open shall these things be and declared to living men." John Harding cites this Mevinus, the British Chronicler, in his versified Chronicle, for whom the name of Nenius appeared in the 48th Chapter: where from him he relates the beautiful story, how that Joseph delivered the Cross to King Arviragus for the insignia of the British race which, afterwards, was called the Georgian Cross, depicted on a silver shield.

latin_text: Verum et otio meo et lectoris patientia abutar, si nugacissima commenta, quæ ex stramentitiis ejusmodi scriptis tum ab Hardingo et Capgravio, tum in magna Glastoniensium tabula de Josepho referuntur, commemorem. Illud minime prætereundum, quod in Europæanorum nostrorum synodis generalibus, quando de Britannici regni dignitate cum Gallis et Hispanis habita est controversia, ad hanc de Josepho traditionem provocare subinde soliti sunt Anglicanæ gentis oratores. Agitata est hæc quæstio anno MCCCCIX. in Pisano primum, deinde anno MCCCCXVII. in Constantiensi concilio : ex quo excerpta est “ Nobilissima disceptatio super dignitate et magnitudine regnorum Britannici et Gallici, habita ab utriusque oratoribus et legatis in concilio Constantiensi,” Lovanii anno MDXVII. typis excusa. Eam ex actis concilii in ipsa urbe Constantiensi asservatis edendam curavit D. Robertus Wingfeldius eques auratus, Henrici VIII. Anglorum regis ad Maximilianum imperatorem orator : quam etiam in duobus MSS. ejusdem concilii exemplaribus invenimus. Hic vero quum in tricesima sessione mota est hæc quæstio : “ an juri et rationi consonum sit, æquiparare regnum Angliæ regno Franciæ, in concilio generali :” pro dignitate Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ, inter alia allegatum est, quod “ Statim post passionem Christi Joseph ab Arimathia, nobilis decurio, qui Christum de

translation_history.english: But I should abuse my leisure and the reader's patience were I to recount the very frivolous fictions which are referred to concerning Joseph in the scattered writings of this kind, now by Harding and Capgrave, now in the "Great Register of Glaston." P al. habitantibus. Jo. Glast. 9 Cap. 50 and 51. That which by no means must be overlooked is that in the General Councils of our Europeans, when a controversy arose touching the dignity of the Kingdom of Britain with the French and Spanish, the ambassadors of the English nation were wont continually to cite this tradition concerning Joseph. This question was deliberated first in the year 1409 in the Council of Pisa, next in the year 1417 in the Council of Constance of which is extracted: ("Nobilissima disceptatio super dignitate et magnitudine regnorum Britannici et Gallici, habita ab utriusque oratoribus et legatis in Concilio Constantiensi. ” Lovanii, anno M.DXVII. typis excusa). "The most celebrated dispute touching the dignity and rank of the kingdoms of Britain and Gaul, maintained by their ambassadors and legates in the Council of Constance. Louvain. Printed in the year 1517. " D. Robertus Wingfeldius, Knight, Ambassador of Henry VIII, King of England, to the Emperor Maximilian, caused this to be published from the recorded acts of the Council of Constance itself, which also we find in the two MSS. transcripts of that Council. r (translated ). Another of these is to be found in the Royal library; another (which formerly had been the property of Cardinal Peter Bembi) in the private one of D. Henry Wotton, v. cl. Here, indeed, when in the 30th session this question was moved "whether it accords with right and reason to put on an equality the kingdom of England and the kingdom of France in General Council ": on behalf of the authority of the English Church it was, among other things, alleged that "Immediately after the Passion of Christ, Joseph of Arimathea, a noble Decurion, who took down Christ from the Cross, with xii companions immediately proceeded to cultivate the Lord's vineyard, that is to say England, and converted the peoples to the faith. To whom the king assigned xii hides of land in the Diocese of Bath for their maintenance: who, so it is written, are buried in the Monastery of Glaston in the diocese of Bath, concerning which xii hides aforementioned the said Monastery is distinguished as having been endowed from ancient times. But the kingdom of France received the faith of Christ in the time of Saint Dionysius and by his ministry."

latin_text: Idem etiam in Senensi concilio anno MCCCCXXIV.

translation_history.english: The same claim also was propounded in the Council of Siena in the year 1424 by Richard Fleming, Bishop of Lincoln and founder of Lincoln College, Oxford, when this controversy was renewed by the English against the Spanish, Scots and French before Martin V.

latin_text: a Richardo Flemmingo Lincolniensi episcopo et Lincolniensis collegii apud Oxonienses conditore, propositum est: quum adversus Hispanos, Scotos et Gallos coram Martino V. ab Anglis renovata esset hæc controversia. Sed in Basileensi præcipue concilio, anno MCCCCXXXIV. inter oratores regis Angliæ et Castellæ efferbuit hæc contentio : ubi quæ nostris hac in parte ab Alphonso Garsia de sancta Maria, legum doctore ac Compostellanæ et Segobiensis ecclesiarum decano, objecta sunt, ex schedis Cottonianis visum est proponere, et excutere. “Oratores regis Angliæ,” ait ille, “tam in præsentia vestrarum reverendissimarum paternitatum, quam in sacra deputatione reformatorii, dixerunt præferendos se propter antiquiorem susceptionem fidei Christianæ. Nam dicunt, quod ille nobilis decurio Joseph ab Arimathia una cum aliis, anno XV. post assumptionem gloriosæ virginis Mariæ venit in Angliam, et magnam ejus partem ad fidem Christi convertit.

translation_history.english: s (translated ). Very nearly the same things may be read in the Book concerning the provinces of England, MS. in the Cottonian Library. But in the Council of Basle especially, in the year 1434, this contention boiled up between the Ambassadors of the King of England and Castile: where, with regard to the objections which had been raised against ours on this question by Alphonso Garcia de Sancta Maria, doctor of laws and Dean of the Churches of Compostella and Segovia, it seemed good to set forth and print them from the Cottonian papers. "The Ambassadors of the King of England," said he, "as well in the presence of your most reverend worships as in the sacred deputation said that they were to be preferred on account of their more ancient reception of the Christian faith. For they say how that that noble Decurion Joseph of Arimathea with others, in the year XV after the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, came into England and converted its greater part to the faith of Christ.

latin_text: Et post non longo tempore a passione Christi, Eleutherius papa regnum Angliæ totaliter convertit ad fidem.”

translation_history.english: And, afterwards, not a long time after the Passion of Christ, Pope Eleutherius converted the whole of the kingdom of England to the faith."

latin_text: Ad primum vero illud de Josepho respondet. I. “Per interemptionem. Nego enim (inquit) Joseph illum venisse in Angliam. Ille ergo qui dicit, probat: (juxta l. Ei qui ff. de proba.) Producatur ergo in medium aliqua historia vel scriptura authentica. II. Per probabilitatem contrariam. Nam licet ei qui negat non incumbat probatio: (ut l. actor. C. de proba.) tamen interdum probatur negativa per judicium; quando habet comitantiam temporum. (ut l. optimam C. contrahentium et com. stipu.)

translation_history.english: To the first, namely that concerning Joseph, he answers: I. "By way of settling that claim, I entirely deny (said he) that Joseph came into England. He who asserts it should prove it (juxta l.Ei qui ff.de proba). Some history or authentic writing should be produced in evidence. II. "On the contrary probability. For though the onus of proof does not lie on him who denies (utl. actor. C.de proba ): yet sometimes the negative is proved by investigation, when it has chronological congruity (ut 1. optimam C. contrahentium et com. stipu.

latin_text: In hoc ergo casu bene potest probari hæc negativa per scripturam contrariam. Continetur enim in floribus sanctorum, sub legenda Jacobi minoris, contrarium. Hoc legitur quoque quod Titus intrans Hierusalem, quemdam murum densissimum vidit, ipsumque perforari jussit: et intus quendam senem repererunt, qui dixit se esse Joseph ab Arimathia, et se ibidem esse inclusum a Judæis quia Christum sepelisset, et quod usque ad tempus istud cœlesti cibo sit pastus. In evangelio tamen Nicodemi dicitur, quod Christus eum liberavit post resurrectionem suam, et in Arimathiam duxit. Potest autem dici quod eductus cum a prædicatione non cessaret, iterum sit ab ipsis Judæis inclusus. Hæc ubi supra. Cum ergo Joseph fuerit incarceratus tanto tempore apud Jerusalem, impossibile est eum fuisse in Anglia, cum sit magna distantia.

translation_history.english: ). In this case, therefore, this negative can well be proved by contrary writings. For the contrary is contained in the Flowers of the Saints, under the Legend of James the Less. "Here it is also read that Titus entering into Jerusalem, saw that a certain wall was very thick, and ordered it to be pierced: and within they discovered a certain old man, who said he was Joseph of Arimathea, and that he had been imprisoned in that place by the Jews on account of his having buried Christ, and that even to that time he had been nourished on heavenly food. "Nevertheless, in the Gospel of Nicodemus it is said that Christ liberated him after his resurrection and conducted him into Arimathea. But it may be said that though released, when he ceased not to preach, he was imprisoned a second time by the Jews themselves. See as to this above. When, therefore, Joseph was imprisoned at such a time at Jerusalem it is impossible for him to have been in England, at so great a distance.

latin_text: III. Potest dici, quod licet hoc fuisset verum, (quod tamen non fuit) non sequitur ergo quod totum solium illud suscepit fidem. IV. Dicitur, dato illo quod negatur, adhuc tamen Hispani primo susceperunt fidem, quod probatur, quia Jacobus martyrium subiit vivente Petro. Scriptum est enin de Herode, quod occidit Jacobum gladio, et apposuit ut apprehenderet Petrum, Actuum capite duodecimo. Sed constat, quod Petrus passus est sub Nerone.

translation_history.english: III. "It may be said, that even though this t (translated ). Or in the Acts of Pilate in Gregory of Tours. histor., lib. 1, cap. 20. were true (which, nevertheless, was not) it does not follow that that whole dominion received the faith. IV. "It is still affirmed, moreover, granted that which is denied, the Spanish first received the faith, which is proved, because James suffered martyrdom in the life of Peter. For it is written of Herod, that he slew James with the sword, and had the intention to apprehend Peter, Chapter XII of the Acts. But it is well known that Peter suffered under Nero.

latin_text: Nero autem fuit prope annum Domini LIV. et Titus fuit prope annum Domini LXXX. Jam certum est quod si Joseph fuisset in Anglia, hoo fuisset postquam de carcere fuisset liberatus per Titum, et sic post octogesimum annum a nativitate Domini: et Jacobus mortuus est ante Neronem pluribus annis, quasi prope quadragesimum annum a nativitate Domini. Et Hispania suscepit fidem a Jaoobo, vivente eo, vel statim in sepultura ejus; ut supra dixi. Ergo Hispania est in fide antiquior." Hæc ad patres Basileensis concilii Alphonsus Garsias: in quibus quædam sunt levia admodum, nonnulla etiam oppido ridicula.

translation_history.english: Nero, moreover, was about the year of Our Lord 54 and Titus about the year 80. Now it is certain that if Joseph were in England, this was after he was liberated from prison by Titus, and thus after the 80th year from the Nativity of Our Lord: and James died many years before Nero, about the 40th year from the Lord's nativity. "And Spain received the faith from James, in his lifetime, or immediately on his burial; as above stated. Therefore Spain is the more ancient in the faith." Thus Alphonsus Garcias to the Fathers at the Council of Basle: wherein some things are wholly trivial, not a few exceedingly ridiculous.

latin_text: Ad primam ejus responsionem quod attinet: historias et scripta antiqua Josephi ad Britannos legationem confirmantia, quanta potuimus diligentia superius collegimus, atque in medium produximus. Quibus jam addimus oratorum et legatorum regis Angliæ, in hac ipsa synodo propositam assertionem. "Certum est in Anglia reperiri in libris antiquissimis et archivis, præcipue in archivis abbatiæ notabilis Glastonensis, diocesis Bathoniensis; quod Joseph ab Arimathia cum duodecim sociis, aut ex persecutione Herodiana, vel præsidum Romanorum in Judæa, ad Angliam vectus est. Ibidem, quæ de Christo viderat et audierat prædicavit, et prædicando plures convertit; convertendo, multa et infinita sibi, ab illis quos converterat ad fidem collata, conquæsivit; conquæsita postea templo Christo per eum erecto reliquit: (et hoc, tempore quo Petrus in Antiochia prædicavit fidem:) quod templum a Joseph erectum, in locum religiosum et abbatialem dignitatem translatum est, et laus Christi per notabile monasterium præservatur ad præsens."

translation_history.english: In regard to his first reply: the histories and ancient writings corroborating the mission of Joseph to the British, we have brought together above with as much diligence as we could, and have produced in evidence. To which we now add the declaration put forward in that Council by the Ambassadors and Legates of the King of England: “Certain it is that in England are to be found in the most ancient books and archives, principally in the archives of the notable Abbey of Glaston, in the diocese of Bath; that Joseph of Arimathea with twelve companions, either in consequence of the persecution of Herod, or of the Roman Governors of Judea, sailed to England. There he preached what he had seen and heard concerning Christ, and by his preaching converted many; and converting them he acquired for himself an infinite number of things collected by those he had converted to the faith; these acquisitions he afterwards left to a Church erected by his means to Christ (and this at the time that Peter preached the faith at Antioch ): which Church, erected by Joseph, has developed into a place of religion and of the dignity of an Abbey, and by means of a notable monastery the praise of Christ is preserved to the present time."

latin_text: Probabilitatem contrariam, quam secundo loco urget, negamus omnino esse probabilem. Neque enim aliquem hodie, si Thomam Dempsterum exceperis, tam stulte credulum esse existimamus, cui absurdissimum illud commentum, de Josepho muro incluso, probabile videri possit: et de legendæ aureæ authore Jacobo de Voragine, ex cujus areolis fœtidi isti sanctorum flores sunt decerpti, in ipsa Hispania a Ludovico Vive et Melchiore Cano jamdudum lata est sententia; ferrei oris eum virum fuisse, atque plumbei cordis.

translation_history.english: We entirely deny that the contrary probability which he urges in the second place, is probable. Nor do we think that anyone to -day, if Thomas Dempster be excepted, " is so foolishly credulous u Apparat, ad histor. Scot, lib. 1, cap. 7, pag. 27; Vid. Melchiorem Inchofer, de veritate epistolae B. Mariae ad Messanenses, cap. 13, pag. 71, 72. as to regard as probable this very absurd fabrication concerning Joseph of Arimathea shut up in a wall; and concerning the author of the "Golden Legend", Jacobo de Voragine," from whose garden plots these fetid Flowers of the Saints are gathered, in Spain itself the opinion is expressed now and has been for a long time. past by Ludovicus Vives and Melchiore Cano that that man was brazen of speech and leaden of heart.

latin_text: Tertium illud, quod totum Britanniæ regnum Josephi ministerio fidem non susceperit; verum quidem est, sed ad rem non pertinet. Nam nec totum regnum Hispaniæ a Jacobo conversum fuisse ipsi Hispani dicent; nec integra regna ab ullo apostolorum Christiana facta esse constat: et de antiquitate, non de universalitate susceptionis fidei instituta est quæstio.

translation_history.english: As to the third point, that the whole of the realm of Britain did not receive the faith by the ministry of Joseph, it is true enough but it is not relevant to the issue. For neither do the Spanish themselves say that the whole kingdom of Spain was converted by James; nor is it established that whole kingdoms were made Christian by any one of the Apostles: and, moreover, the question at issue concerns the antiquity, not the universality, of the reception of the faith.

latin_text: Quartum vero et postremum, partim incertis, partim falsis nititur fundamentis. Jacobi prædicationem in Hispania, inter incerta posuit Rodericus Ximenius Toletanus archiepiscopus, in concertatione quam anno MCCXV. in Lateranensi concilio cum præsule Compostellano de primatu habuit. Ejus verba, a Garsia Loaisa e libro MS. bibliothecæ Toletanæ edita, hæc sunt. “ Si inducat (Compostellanus) primam divini verbi promulgationem, et plurimorum conversionem ad fidem Christi in Hispania (per Jacobum factam:) qui divinam paginam noverunt, testimonium perhibeant. Ego tantum legi, datam ei fuisse potestatem prædicandi in Hispania: sed interim, cum per Judæam et Samariam divinam legem seminaret, sub Herode Hierosolymis truncato capite exhalavit animam, et Domino reddidit. Quomodo ergo ibi prædicavit, quo nondum ingressus est? aut sine prædicatione, quos, obsecro, convertit ad Dominum?” Nec ex parte altera certum est, quantumvis id ita esse affirmet Alphonsus, “ quod si Joseph fuisset in Anglia, hoc fuisset postquam de carcere liberatus fuisset per Titum, et sic post octuagesimum annum a nativitate Domini.” A Tito enim, anno æræ Christianæ (non octogesimo sed) septuagesimo eversam esse Hierosolymam certum est: quæ vero de Josepho Arimathæensi tunc per eum liberato pro certis assumuntur, nugæ sunt nugerrimæ.

translation_history.english: As to the fourth and last point, this rests partly upon doubtful, and partly upon false, premises. Rodericus Ximensis, Archbishop of Toledo, accounted the preaching of James in Spain as doubtful, in the controversy which he had in the year 1215, in the Lateran Council with the Prefect of Compostella, concerning the w Jacob. Januens, in legenda S. Jacobi minoris. * Vives, de causis corrupt. artium. lib. 2. y Can. de locis Theolog. lib. 11., cap. 6. primacy. His words, published by Garsia Loaisa from the MS. book of the Toledo Library, are: "If he (Compostellanus ) brings forward the first promulgation of the Divine Word and the conversion of very many to the faith of Christ in Spain (accomplished by James ), let them who are acquainted with Holy Writ produce the evidence. I only know that the opportunity was given him of preaching in Spain: but, in the meantime, while sowing the Divine Word through Judea and Samaria, he was decapitated under Herod at Jerusalem and giving up the Ghost, rendered it unto his Lord. How, therefore, did he preach there where he had not been at all? or whom, pray, without preaching, did he convert to the Lord?” Nor on the other hand is it certain, however much Alphonsus may affirm it to be so, "That if Joseph was in England, it was after he had been liberated from prison by Titus, and so after the 80th year from the Lord's Nativity. For it is certain that Jerusalem was destroyed by Titus in the 70th year (not the 80th ) of the Christian era: in fact, that which is assumed as certain concerning Joseph of Arimathea being liberated by him is an idle tale of the most frivolous character. z Collect. Concil. Hispan, a Loaisa edit., pag. 291; et Concil. edit. Colon.

latin_text: Guilielmus quidem Eysengreineus ex annalibus Anglorum narrat eum “ post urbis Hierosolymæ destructionem apostolis adhæsisse; atque hoc pacto jam senem in Britanniam profectum, in urbe Wellia Christum prædicavisse.” Sed temporis illam circumstantiam in nullis Anglorum annalibus expressam reperit. Glastonienses, et Malmesburiensis monachus in secundo Eulogii sui libro, Josephi adventum ad annum Christi LXIII. referunt: quem ab assumptione beatæ virginis XV. fuisse tradunt.

translation_history.english: an. 1618, tom. 2, part 2, pag. 317, 318. Vide Baron. annal., tom. 9., an. 816., sec. 49, 50, 51, 52, et bibliothec. Floriacens. Joannis Certainly William Eysengreineusª in his annals of the English relates that he "after the destruction of Jerusalem attached himself to the Apostles: and that, by agreement, he proceeded to Britain when he was now old, and preached Christ in the city of Wells." But in no English annals does he find that express circumstance as to time. The Glastonians, and the monk of Malmesbury in the second book of his Eulogy, refer the coming of Joseph to the year of Christ 63: which they propound as the fifteenth from the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin.

latin_text: Oratores Angli, ut diximus, in Basileensi hoc concilio, templum a Josepho in Britannia erectum asserunt, “ tempore quo Petrus in Antiochia prædicavit fidem :” et in Constantiensi, “ statim post passionem Christi” eundem Britanniam ingressum esse, et populos ad fidem convertisse defendunt. Quod et cum ipsius Josephi ætate, qui Domino passionem adeunte inter Judæos senator honoratus fuerat, et cum iis quæ initio ex Gilda de tempore summo Tiberii Cæsaris produximus, bene quadrat.

translation_history.english: The English Ambassadors, as we have said, claim in this Council of Basle that a Church had been erected by Joseph in Britain " at the time when Peter preached the faith in Antioch ": and in the Council of Constance, they maintained that "immediately after the Passion of Christ " he entered Britain and converted the people to the faith. Which well agrees both with the age of Joseph himself, who when the Lord was entering upon his Passion, had been an honoured senator among the Jews, and with those things which at the commencement we produced from a Eysengrein. cent. 1, part 6, distinct. 6. b Mar.

latin_text: Johannes enim Hardingius indignus est, cujus hic ulla habeatur ratio : qui Josephum per ipsos quadraginta duos a Christi morte annos, non quidem in muro, sed in Caiphæ carcere detentum, sine omni cibo et potu vixisse ; deinde a Vespasiano liberatum, et in Britanniam anno Christi LXXVI. perductum, ibique regi Arvirago et conjugi ipsius Genissæ (quæ Claudii imperatoris filia fuisse fingitur) commendatum fuisse fabulatur. Johannes Balæus, Ossoriensis aliquando apud Hibernos episcopus, eodem illo anno ex vita hac migrasse eum scribit. “ In sancta senectute (inquit) Josephus inter discipulos tandem quietam morte carnis dormitionem accepit, in Avalonica solitudine sepultus, anno a Christi incarnatione LXXVI. Mario regnante in Britannia. Postea translatum est ejus corpus ad Glasconiense monachorum collegium, et in pretiosa theca repositum. Neque desunt (inquit ille) qui ex conjecturis habeant, contexuisse illum ad ecclesias Britannorum epistolas quasdam.” Quam conjecturam ut verisimiliorem redderet Guilielmus Eysengreineus, ne a præsente ad præsentes literæ scriptæ putarentur, “ reliquisse insulam et, ut renovaret sui memoriam, scripsisse epistolam ad Britannos” illum fingit: Anglorum hic quoque citatis annalibus ; in quibus tamen neque Britanniam eum reliquisse, neque ejusmodi aliquam epistolam scripsisse, neque alibi quam Glastoniæ mortuum et sepultum fuisse, uspiam traditum invenimus.

translation_history.english: cap. 15., ver. 43. evoxýμwv Bovλeuròs quod a vulgato interprete, nobilis decurio, redditur, de quo videndus commentarius B. Hieronymi in Matth., cap. 27., et Ludovici de Dieu V.C. in Marc., cap. 15. Et. H. Grotii, in Matth., cap. 27., ver. 57. Qui apud Plinium Secundum, lib. 10, epist. 113. Buleutae in Rescripto Trajani, epist. 114. decuriones appellantur. Gildas concerning the last days of Tiberias Cæsar. For John Harding does not deserve that any respect should be paid to him here: who pretends that Joseph for these forty -two years from the death of Christ, lived, not indeed in a wall, but detained in the prison of Caiaphas, without food or drink: that then he was liberated by Vespasian and brought over to Britain in the year of Christ 76 and that there he was commended to the king Arviragus and his wife Genissa (who is represented as being the daughter of the Emperor Claudius ). John Bale, sometime Bishop of Ossory in Ireland, writes that he departed this life in that same year. " In sainted old age (he says )ª Joseph at length in the midst of his disciples by the death of the body gained the sleep of peace, being buried in the solitude of Avalon in the year 76 from Christ's Incarnation and in the reign of Marius in Britain. Afterwards his body was translated to the College of the Monks of Glaston and enclosed in a casket of great price. Nor are there wanting (says he) those who from conjectures maintain that he composed a certain Epistle to the British churches." Which conjecture William Eysengreineus, that he might render it more probable, and that the epistle might not be regarded as written by one present to those present, pretends that he " had left the island and in order to keep his memory green, had written an Epistle to the British": here, too, with a quotation from the Annals of the English: in which, however, we find it nowhere stated that he had either left Britain or written any letter of the kind or had died and been buried elsewhere than at Glaston.

latin_text: Extat vetustus catalogus sanctorum in Anglia sepultorum Saxonice scriptus, ac Latine, a Gotcelino Bertiniano monacho Cantuariensi, Anselmi archiepiscopi diebus editus: et de reliquis in Glastoniensi monasterio repositis libellus alter, Henrici III. Anglorum regis temporibus exaratus. In neutro vero Josephi ulla occurrit mentio.

translation_history.english: There exists a very ancient register of Saints buried in England, written in the Saxon tongue, and in Latin, by Gotcelinus Bertinianus, a monk of Canterbury, published in the days of Archbishop Anselm: and another book concerning the relics preserved at the Monastery of Glaston, discovered in the times of Henry III, King of England. In neither, indeed, does any mention occur of Joseph.

latin_text: Anno demum MCCCXLV. a Johanne Blomæo Londinensi, cujusdam revelationis sibi factæ prætextu, ab Edvardo III. licentia quærendi corpus Josephi ab Arimathia impetrata est: quam, ex archivis regiis in arce Londinensi asservatis a me descriptam, lectori communicare non gravabor.

translation_history.english: At length, in the year 1345, a license was procured from Edward III by John Blome of London on the pretext of a certain revelation made to him, to seek for the body of Joseph of Arimathea: which, as transcribed by me from the royal archives preserved in the Tower of London, I do not think it amiss to communicate to the reader: e Septoniæ enim sepultum fuisse (ea Dorsettensium Shaftesburia est) per errorem scriptum legitur in Jo.

latin_text: “Rex omnibus ad quos, &c. salutem. Supplicavit nobis Johannes Blome de London, ut cum sibi (sicut asserit) divinitus sit injunctum, ut venerandum corpus decurionis nobilis Josephi ab Arimathia, quod infra septa monasterii Glastoniensis in Christo quiescit humatum, et est ad honorem et multorum ædificationem his temporibus revelandum, quærat donec inveniat diligenter. Et quia in quibusdam antiquis scripturis dicitur contineri corpus ejus ibidem fuisse sepultum. Nos, si sit ita, desiderantes monumentum ejus, et venerandas ipsius reliquias, qui redemptori nostro morienti tantum exhibebat pietatis et humanitatis obsequium, corpus ejus de cruce deponendo, et illud in monumento suo novo ponendo, devotis honoribus prævenire; et sperantes nobis et toti regno nostro ex revelatione prædicta gratiam uberiorem provenire: concessimus et licentiam dedimus (quantum in nobis est) eidem Johanni quod ipse infra præcinctum dicti monasterii fodere, et illas prætiosas reliquias juxta injunctionem et revelationem sibi factam quærere valeat in locis ubi melius viderit expedire: dum tamen absque damno dilectorum nobis in Christo, abbatis et conventus dicti monasterii, et ruina ecclesiæ et domorum suarum ibidem id fieri valeat; et quod ad id ipsorum abbatis et conventus licentiam habeat et assensum. In cujus, &c. Teste Rege PER IPSUM REGEM.

translation_history.english: Caii historiae Cantabriq., lib. I, pag. 23, nam. Glasconiæ, ibidem, pag. 31. legitur. "The King to all to whom & c. Greeting. John Blome of London has petitioned us, that, whereas it has been divinely imposed upon him (as he asserts ), in order that the body of the noble decurion Joseph of Arimathea, which buried beneath the inclosure of the Monastery of Glaston rests in Christ, may be venerated and revealed in these times to the honour and edification of many, he may diligently seek until he find it. And because in certain ancient writings his body is said to be contained in the spot where it was buried. We, if it be so, being desirous of a memorial of him and of shewing all fitting honours to the venerable remains of him who shewed for our dying Redeemer such homage of piety and humanity in removing His body from the Cross and placing it in his own new tomb; and trusting to produce for ourselves and for our whole nation the greater favour: Concede and grant license (so far as in us lies ) to the same John to dig beneath the precincts of the said Monastery and that it be lawful for him to seek those precious remains according to the charge and revelation made to him in such places as he may think fit: Provided nevertheless that it can be done without detriment to our well beloved in Christ,the Abbot and Chapter of the said Monastery, and without damage totheir Church and dwellings and tothis end he should have the license and assent of the Abbot and Chapter themselves.

latin_text: Apud Westmonaster.

translation_history.english: At Westminster

latin_text: VIII. die Junii.

translation_history.english: VIII day of June.

latin_text: Quem habuerit eventum ista inquisitio, non invenio: ab his tamen qui Glastoniense monasterium viderunt est proditum, et sacellum ibi Josephi nomini dicatum, et tumulum etiam positum fuisse, hoc inscriptum epitaphio.

translation_history.english: What was the outcome of this enquiry, I do not find: but by those who have seen the Monastery of Glaston it has been handed down, that a chapel was there dedicated to the name of Joseph, and also that a tomb was situated there inscribed with this epitaph:

latin_text: Ad Britones veni, postquam Christum sepelivi; -----------------------------------------docui, requievi.

translation_history.english: "I came to the Britons, after that I had buried Christ: I taught, I found rest."

latin_text: Quibus adde, si libet, et Guilielmi Goodi Jesuitæ narrationem, qui Henrico VIII. regnante Glastoniæ natus et puer educatus est. " Glasconiæ extabant (inquit) laminæ æneæ sculptæ ad perpetuandam memoriam, sacella, crypta, cruces, arma, observatio festi S. Josephi ad VI. Calendas Augusti, quamdiu monachi regum chartis munitissime gaudebant: nunc omnia cum ruinis confusa perierunt.

translation_history.english: To which add also, if you please, the narrative of William Goode the Jesuit, who in the reign of Henry VIII was born at Glaston and was educated there as a boy: "There were in existence (he says ) at Glasconia inscribed tablets of brass to perpetuate his memory, chapels, crypts, crosses, arms, and the observance of the feast of S. Joseph for vi days at the Calends of August, as long as the monks enjoyed most securely the King's Charters: now all things have perished mingled with the ruins.

latin_text: Nemo tamen monachorum unquam scivit certum locum sepulchri hujus sancti, vel designavit. Reconditum abditissime dixerunt, vel ibi, vel in monte, qui monti acuto vicinus, et cui nomen Hamden-hill : et futurum, ut quando reperietur corpus ejus, universus eo mundus confluat præ magnitudine et numero miraculorum quæ fient."

translation_history.english: But none of the monks ever knew the exact position of this holy sepulcre, or described it. They say that it was most carefully concealed, either there, or on a mount, which is in the vicinity of a pointed mountain, and the name of which is Hamden -hill: and that some day his body will be found, and that the whole world will flock thither because of the greatness and number of the miracles which will be wrought.'

latin_text: " Et inter cætera memini me vidisse Glasconiæ in cruce lapidea, quæ sub regina Elizabetha subversa fuit, laminam æneam in qua scribebatur, Josephum ab Arimathæa trigesimo anno post passionem Christi venisse in Britanniam cum undecim vel duodecim sociis, permissumque ei ab Arvirago rege, Glasconiæ quæ tunc erat insula dicta Avalonia, habitare, tanquam solitarios viros et simplices : et quod attulerit secum duo vasa argentea non grandia, in quibus erat de sanguine et aqua sacratissima, quæ profluxerat de latere Christi mortui. Crux autem ista erecta est ante multos annos ad denotandam longitudinem sacelli ab eodem sancto Josepho ex vimineis cratibus constructi in honorem beatissimæ virginis; deducta scilicet linea recta a medio illius crucis ad latus sacelli postea lapidibus quadratis exædificati: sub qua item erat olim illud sacellum Sancti Josephi in crypta subterranea. Foris autem in muro hujus sacelli beatæ virginis erant in lapide sculpta vetustissimis literis hæc duo verba, Jesus, Maria. Et confirmant antiqua arma Glasconiensis monasterii, quæ sunt hujusmodi: Scutum album in quo per longum erigitur stipes crucis viridis et nodosæ, et de latere ad latus extenduntur brachia seu rami crucis stipiti consimilia.

translation_history.english: "And, among other things, I remember to have seen at Glasconia on a stone cross, which was overturned under Queen Elizabeth, a brass tablet on which was inscribed, that Joseph of Arimathea came to Britain in the thirtieth year after the Passion of Christ with eleven or twelve companions, and that he was allowed by King Arviragus to dwell at Glasconia which was then an island called Avalonia, as solitary and simple men: and that he brought with him two silver vases of no great size in which was some of the most holy blood and water which had flowed from the side of the dead Christ. Moreover this same cross was erected many years before to denote the length of the chapel constructed by the aforesaid St. Joseph of willow wattles in honour of the Blessed Virgin: to wit, with a straight line drawn from the middle of the Cross to the side of the Chapel that was afterwards built of squared stones: under which hvid. supr., pag. 31, et 37. was also once the Chapel of St. Joseph in a subterranean crypt. Moreover outside in the wall of this Chapel of the Blessed Virgin there were carved in stone in characters of great age these two words, JESUS, MARIA. And the ancient arms of the Monastery of Glasconia confirm this, which are as follows: A white shield on which longways is erected the shaft of a green and knotty cross and from side to side are stretched arms or branches of the cross similar to the shaft.

latin_text: Sparguntur guttæ sanguinis per omnem aream scuti.

translation_history.english: Drops of blood are sprinkled all over the surface of the shield.

latin_text: Utrinque ad latera stipitis, et sub alis crucis, ponitur ampulla inaurata. Et hæc semper denominabantur insignia Sancti Josephi: qui ibi habitasse pie credebatur, et fortasse sepultus esse.”

translation_history.english: On each side of the shaft and under the arms of the Cross is placed a gilded chalice. And these were always denominated the insignia of St. Joseph who was piously believed to have lived, and probably to have been buried there."

latin_text: Eundem cum sociis ibi fuisse sepultum, in magna Glastoniensium tabula ita traditum invenio. “ Ibi requiescunt XII. discipuli: quorum primas et custos fuit Joseph ab Arimathia, qui Dominum sepelivit. Multi ex paganis per eos ad fidem Christi conversi ac baptizati ibidem requiescunt, quorum, propter eorum multitudinem, non est numerus.” De iisdem eulogii author, libro secundo: “ Ibidem diu commorantes, multisque de dicto regno ad locum confluentibus per eosdem ad Christum conversis, tandem in pace quieverunt. Joseph vero ab Arimathia ibidem sepultus est juxta dictam Ecclesiam [B. Mariæ] cum duabus phialis plenis de sudore Christi sanguineo, quas secum de terra sancta detulerat.” Quis vero inde usque ad Lucii regis tempora loci illius status fuerit, Guilielmus Malmesburienſis his verbis edocet. “Sancti igitur memorati in eadem eremo sic degentes, eﬄuentibus multis annorum curriculis carnis ergastulo sunt educti: idemque locus cœpit esse ferarum latibulum, qui prius fuerat habitatio sanctorum.”

translation_history.english: That the aforesaid Joseph was buried there with his companions, I find thus recorded in the "Great Register of the Monks of Glaston:" "Here repose xii disciples: of whom the head and guardian was Joseph of Arimathea, who buried the Lord. Many from among the pagans converted by their means to the faith of Christ and baptized rest in the same spot, of whom on account of their multitude, there is no number." Concerning these pagans the author of the "Eulogy " in his second book says: "Sojourning here for a long time, and many flocking from the said kingdom to the spot having been converted to Christ by their means, at length they rested in peace. Moreover Joseph of Arimathea was buried in the same spot close to the aforesaid church of the Blessed Mary with two phials full of the bloody sweat of Christ, which he had brought with him from the Holy Land." Now, what was the condition of the place from that time to the times of King Lucius, William of Malmesbury tells us in these words: "So these renowned holy men ' thus dwelling in this same wilderness, after many fleeting years had run their course, were released from the prison house of the flesh: and the same place began to be the lair of wild beasts which before had been the habitation of Saints."
